title: Trace-the-Data Investigation (Lab)
summary: Students run three controlled single data swaps on the ripeness sorter, log the before-and-after outcomes, and use that evidence to identify and verify the most influential change.
objectives: Change the data in a worked solution and observe and record the effect on the outcome.
Identify which single data change most alters the outcome, and explain why.

body: In the Core lesson you predicted how a data change would move the outcome. A prediction is only a guess until you test it. Today you run a fair test: change one thing, watch the outcome, and let the evidence tell you which data matters most.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run a controlled data change and record the outcome before and after.
I can compare data changes and identify which one moved the outcome the most.
I can explain, using my recorded evidence, why that change had the biggest effect.

terms.definition: Changing one thing at a time so you know what caused the result.
The outcome measured just before and just after a single change.
How far the outcome moved because of a change.
Having a large effect on the outcome.
To re-test and confirm an effect is real, not a one-off.

sections.heading: Change one thing at a time
body: To find out how much a data batch matters, you must isolate it. Measure the outcome **before**, change only that one batch, and measure again. The difference is the influence of that batch.
If you change two batches at once and the outcome moves, you cannot tell which batch did it. A fair test changes one variable at a time - the same rule scientists use in any experiment.

sections.heading: Evidence beats opinion
body: Your log is your evidence. Without a written before-and-after, you are relying on memory, and memory blurs across many swaps.

Once you have run several swaps, the most [[influential]] batch is the one with the biggest [[shift]]. [[Verify]] it by re-running on a fresh fruit - if the effect repeats, you have proof, not a coincidence.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Work in threes with roles: swapper, recorder, checker. You will run three single data swaps, log each outcome, and find the most influential change.
items: Write your Core prediction at the top of the log.
Record the BEFORE outcome for your test fruit.
Swap in one data batch and record the AFTER outcome.
Note the shift: none, a little, or a lot.
Repeat for two more single swaps.
Rank the swaps and star the most influential.
Verify the winner on a fresh fruit and write your conclusion.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Did the evidence match your prediction? Where did it surprise you?
Why might a small batch beat a large one for influence?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write your evidence-based conclusion about the most influential data change.
Note one thing a fair test taught you that a guess could not.

questions.prompt: A group swapped in the green-date batch AND the yellow-date batch at the same time. The sorter's answer changed from 'ripe' to 'unripe'. What should they write in their log?

options.text: We cannot tell which batch moved the outcome, so we will redo the test changing one batch at a time.
Both batches are equally influential, because the outcome moved when we swapped them together.
The larger batch caused the change, because a bigger batch always has the bigger effect.
The test worked fine - swapping two batches at once saves time and gives us the same evidence.

feedback.correct: Right - with two changes at once the result cannot be attributed to either batch, so the fair test has to be run again one batch at a time.
feedback.incorrect: When two batches change together the shift could have come from either one, or from both; only a single controlled swap tells you which batch did it.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of one fair data-swap test into the order you should carry them out.

items.text: Swap in one data batch, and only that batch.
Record the outcome for your test fruit before you change anything.
Re-run the winning swap on a fresh fruit to check the effect repeats.
Compare the two recorded outcomes and write down the size of the shift.
Record the outcome for the same test fruit again.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the 'before' has to be recorded first, or there is nothing to compare the 'after' with, and verifying comes last.
feedback.incorrect: A fair test records the before outcome first, changes one batch, records the after outcome, measures the shift, and only then verifies the winner on a fresh fruit.

questions.prompt: Three rows from an investigation log on a sorter trained mostly on brown ripe dates. Match each row to what the evidence in it shows.

left.text: Added 40 more brown ripe photos. Before: 'ripe'. After: 'ripe'.
Added 40 green unripe photos. Before (green date): 'ripe'. After: 'unripe'.
Kept the 40 green unripe photos and tested a second, fresh green date. Before: 'ripe'. After: 'unripe'.

right.text: No influence - the batch repeated a pattern the sorter already had plenty of, so nothing shifted.
Influential - the batch filled a gap in the data and the outcome changed.
Verified - the same change moved the outcome again on a fresh fruit, so the effect is real, not a one-off.

feedback.correct: Well read - a row with no shift shows no influence, a row with a shift shows influence, and a repeat of that shift on a fresh fruit is verification.
feedback.incorrect: Read each row's before and after: no movement means no influence, movement means influence, and the same movement repeating on a fresh fruit is what verifies it.

questions.prompt: True or false: once a swap has moved the outcome one time, that single result is enough proof that the batch is the most influential one - there is no need to test it again.

feedback.correct: Correct - one result could be a coincidence, so you re-run the swap on a fresh fruit to verify the effect repeats.
feedback.incorrect: It is false: a single moved outcome might be a one-off, so you verify by re-running the swap on a fresh fruit and checking the effect happens again.

questions.prompt: Your log shows Swap A: no shift, Swap B: a big shift, Swap C: a little shift, and a re-run of Swap B on a fresh date that shifted the same way. Select ALL the conclusions your evidence actually supports.

options.text: Of the three swaps we tested, Swap B was the most influential, because our log shows it produced the biggest before/after shift.
Swap B's effect is real and not a coincidence, because the re-run on a fresh date moved the outcome the same way.
Swap B is the most influential data change that exists for any sorter anywhere.
Swap A and Swap C can never change the outcome of any solution.
Swap B must be the winner because it is the one we predicted would win before we started.

feedback.correct: Yes - your conclusions stay inside what you actually recorded: the biggest logged shift, confirmed by a repeat run.
feedback.incorrect: A conclusion must not go further than the log: you tested three swaps on one sorter, and a prediction you made beforehand is not evidence - the recorded shifts are.

formative.targets: Grade 4 Advanced: explains how data influences the outcome of a solution
formative.check: Investigation log showing before/after outcomes for several single data swaps, plus a ranked conclusion
formative.successCriteria: Records outcomes for controlled single swaps and identifies, with evidence, the most influential change.
formative.evidence: Completed investigation log + one-sentence evidence-based conclusion.
